minor.issue: 'Iron supplementation is not recommended unless iron deficiency is confirmed' simplifies the source: high-dose (>45 mg/day) iron should not be taken unless deficiency is present, and routine supplementation 'can do more harm than good'.
'without systematic appraisal' is fair because this is not a systematic review, but the authors describe their work as a 'narrative synthesis and critical appraisal'.
The source text is the first online version (Br J Sports Med 2020;0:1-27). The 2021;55:416-442 details cannot be verified from the text.

It is entirely generic, with no quantitative recommendations (6-8 g/kg CHO, 30-60 g/h, 20-25 g protein every 3-4 h, 1.6-2.2 g/kg, vitamin D 2000 IU when deficient), so it does not tell staff what the statement actually says.
It does not mention the level 5 (expert opinion) evidence rating, the reliance on recreational or simulated protocols, the sparse data on female players, or the authors' disclosed industry ties.
It does not mention the 31-member group, the nine topics or the December 2017-December 2019 process.

note: Every specific number in A (6-8 g/kg for 48-72 h, 30-60 g/h, a 1-3 g/kg meal 3-4 h pre-match, 20-25 g protein every 3-4 h, 1.6-2.2 g/kg, 2000 IU D3 if deficient, no LCHF diet, rehab protein >=1.6 g/kg with 20-30 g leucine-rich protein per meal, no proven anti-inflammatory strategy) matches the source, while B is accurate but too generic to act on.
